segments.text: We turn today to Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians.
The first episode of Paul to the Thessalonians, chapter 1 and verse 1.
Paul and Serenus and Timothy to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Grace to you and peace.
Paul includes his two co-workers Silas, whose other name was Serenus, and Timothy in writing this letter.
Even though we know very clearly the letter was dictated and written by Paul himself,
yet we see his humility recognizing that he is a member of the body of Christ,
recognizing that in this New Testament age God has given different gifts to different members,
and that there is to be a corporate expression of Christ through a body.
He graciously and in humility includes Silas and Timothy in the address.
Paul, Silvanus and Timothy to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father
and the Lord Jesus Christ. They are distinguishing between the Father and the Son
as two separate persons of the Trinity, and he says,
Grace to you and peace. This is Paul's common mode of greeting whenever he writes to Christians.
Grace is a distinctively New Testament word. It's rarely found in the Old Testament,
except prophetically as something that was going to come in the New Testament age.
And he says, Grace to you and peace. Two great blessings that come to us through the Gospel.
Grace to forgive us and free us from sin's power.
Peace, which is the result of this forgiveness and this freedom from sin.
In what peace, peace from anxiety, freedom from anxiety,
and peace in the midst of all the trials and ups and downs of life.
Grace to we give thanks to God always for all of you.
It's amazing how Paul could speak like this to the various Christians he wrote,
that he was always giving thanks for them.
There were many weaknesses in many of these Christians,
but Paul had disciplined himself to give thanks to God for the good things
that he could see in many of them. And so he could say, we give thanks to God always
for all of you making mention of you in our prayers.
Paul must have been a tremendous prayer warrior, praying for many Christians.
Almost every church he writes to, he says, I make mention of you in prayer.
In the midst of his busy schedule and his work, he found time
to give thanks to God for these different Christians and to pray for them.
And then he says what he particularly thanks God for
and what he particularly prays for. Verse 3,
constantly bearing in mind your work of faith
and labor of love and steadfastness of perseverance of hope
in our Lord Jesus Christ in the presence of our God and Father.
Notice the three things mentioned in verse 3.
Your work of faith, their faith produced works. It wasn't a dead faith,
a faith which was merely intellectual and theoretical.
It was a faith which produced works of obedience,
works that glorified God. And so he says in verse 3,
your work of faith. And then he speaks of your labor of love.
Their love for Christ produced labor. Their labor was not a labor
that was a dead work. It was a labor of love,
not a labor of duty or because the law demanded it.
It was a labor of love. And their patient endurance
in trial and testing, their perseverance and their steadfastness
in the midst of all their trials was again not something dead,
but something that was a result of the hope that they had. A hope in the Lord
Jesus Christ. And so we see the work of faith,
the labor of love, and the patience, perseverance and endurance
of hope. That hope that one day Christ would come
and they would be like him. And they persevered and endured in trial and
temptation because of this hope that was set
before them. The hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.
And all this was in the presence of God and of our God and Father.
Not in the presence of men. It was not a work of faith done to impress men.
It was not a labor of love done to seek the honor of men or to receive glory
from men. Nor was the patient endurance of hope
something which was for man's honor. It was in the presence of our God and
Father. When we compare this with Revelation
chapter 2 and verse 1 downwards,
we find there in verse 2 particularly, in Paul's letter to
the Lord's letter to the church in Ephesus, he says
verse 2 of Revelation 2, I know your work
and your labor and your perseverance. Notice the contrast between this
and 1 Thessalonians 1.3. In 1 Thessalonians 1.3 we read it as the work of
faith. In the church in Ephesus it had become
just work. In 1 Thessalonians 1.3 it was the labor of love.
In Revelation 2.2 it had become just labor. And in 1 Thessalonians 1.3 it was
the perseverance of hope. In Revelation 2.3 it had become just
perseverance. The faith and love and hope were absent.
No wonder the Lord said to the church in Ephesus
in Revelation 2 verse 4, I have this against you.
You have left your first love. It was also true
that their work was no longer the work of faith. Their labor was not the labor of
love and their patience was not the patience
of hope. But in Thessalonians, Thessalonians where Paul
writes to these Christians, their work was the work of faith.
Their labor was the labor of love and their steadfastness,
their perseverance was the perseverance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.
And then he goes on in verse 4 of 1 Thessalonians 1 to say,
knowing brethren beloved by God, His choice
of you. He emphasizes the fact that it was not
they who chose God but that was God who chose them. Like Jesus said to His
disciples, you have not chosen me but I have
chosen you. Verse 5, our gospel did not come to you
in word only but also in power and in the Holy Spirit
and with full conviction. Just as you know what kind of men
we prove to be among you for your sake. And another translation of this
verse says that our preaching to you did not depend upon mere
human argument. It was not just meaningless words. It was not just mere
words. It came in the power of the Holy
Spirit and with full conviction. And so we see
that when the apostles preached the gospel,
they were not concerned merely to have the facts of the gospel right.
They were not concerned merely to have their words
correct or they were not concerned whether their message was impressive in words
or they did not depend on logical argument.
Our gospel did not come to you in word only.
No doubt they used words, no doubt they used arguments where it was necessary
and forcefulness of words where that was necessary but
underlying it all was the mighty power of the Holy Spirit
who bore witness to those words. There was full conviction in their own
hearts. This is how all our preaching must be.
The preaching of the gospel and the teaching of the word of God must never be
mere words but it must always be in the power of the Holy Spirit
with full conviction that what we are speaking
is the truth of God. And in not only that, we see something else in verse 5.
This preaching in the power of the Holy Spirit was backed up
by a type of life that was worthy of the gospel.
So notice the three things in verse 5. There was the message
of the gospel in the words spoken. There was the power of the Holy Spirit
backing up those words and conviction that came as a result of that.
And thirdly, there was the life of the messenger that backed up the message
they preached. He says in the last part of verse 5,
just as you know, what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.
The preacher of the gospel is called not only to present the truth
of the gospel but also to live in such a manner
that people can be attracted, that people can see
that this gospel has done a work in the life of the messenger.
And that's why in verse 6 he could say to the personalians,
you became imitators of us and of the Lord. And this is a question that everyone
who preaches the gospel needs to ask himself.
Do I preach the message of the gospel correctly, first of all?
Second, do I preach it in the power of the Holy Spirit?
And third, do I preach it with a life that I can call others to examine
and say here is something you can imitate?
And here is where we find the sad life today, where we need to repent
and turn to God and say, Lord, make our lives worthy
of the gospel that we preach. We turn now to one Thessalonians and chapter 1
and verse 6. We were considering in our last study
how the gospel was preached by Paul in word, verse 5, in the power of the
Holy Spirit and with a life that was worthy of
the gospel, backing it up. Therefore, he could call the Thessalonians
to be followers of him and of the Lord. Paul writes the same thing to the
Christians in Corinth. Be followers of me, to the Christians in
Philippi. Be followers of me. This was something that
he was not ashamed to say because he had a life
that manifested the truth of the gospel. It's a very sad thing when a preacher
of the gospel cannot say, be followers of me. When a
person has to say, don't look at me, but look at Christ,
you know there's something fundamentally wrong with his preaching.
Why should we not look at him if the gospel
has not produced a change in his life? It's no use
listening to the gospel preached by such a man.
Paul could say to the Thessalonians, you became imitators of us
and in becoming imitators of us or followers of us,
you followed in the steps of our Lord because Paul
and Serenus and Timothy were following in the footsteps of Christ.
And what was the result of their receiving this gospel?
Verse 6, having received the word in much tribulation
and with the joy of the Holy Spirit. The early Christians
face tribulation constantly, particularly from religious Jews,
but later on also from the Romans because they would not
acknowledge Caesar as Lord. They would only say that Jesus Christ is Lord.
So tribulation was a very common experience for most Christians
in the first century, but this did not rob them of their joy.
In fact, it increased their joy. Tribulation worked
perseverance in them and Paul could say to the Romans, Romans 5,
we exalt in tribulation. Romans 5 verse 3, because we know that
tribulation is producing an us proven character.
And so we see that the Thessalonians Christians, they were very young,
but they had the joy of the Holy Spirit. You don't need to be a mature Christian
to have the joy of the Holy Spirit. No, you can have the joy of the Holy Spirit
in the midst of tribulation if you are a follower
in the footsteps of the Lord. And because of this, verse 7,
the Thessalonians became an example to the other believers in Macedonia
and in Achaia. Notice this progression. First of all, verse 6, Paul became an
example to the Thessalonians Christians. Sylvanus and Timothy, having seen
Paul's example, followed Paul's example, they also became examples to the
Thessalonians Christians. Verse 6, the Thessalonians Christians could follow the
example of Paul, Silas and Timothy. And because they followed their example
and they were following the Lord, the Thessalonians Christians, their lives also
became worthy of following. And so they in turn became an example
to the other believers, verse 7, in Macedonia and Achaia.
This is God's will for us. But when we follow in the footsteps of Jesus,
other people younger to us can see our example and follow us.
And other people younger to them can see their example and follow them.
So the gospel is not just something that we are to preach as a doctrine and as a
message, but also back up with a life which we
can call others to follow. And further, we read here in verse 8,
For the word of the Lord has sounded forth from you,
not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward
God has gone forth, so that we have no need to say anything.
It was not just the example of their lives, which was spreading the sweet
fragrance of Christ in Macedonia and Achaia and other places.
But God doesn't save people by the foolishness of a godly life.
No. We're told very clearly in 1 Corinthians chapter 1
that it is by the foolishness of preaching or the word or the message
preached. So we don't go overboard on either side,
as though the message only is important or the life only is important.
It's the life plus the message. When Paul came to Thessalonica, he had a godly life,
but he opened his mouth and preached. And that's why he says in verse 5,
It was with my life, but also with my word, not in word only.
And the same example was followed by the Thessalonians. They lived a godly life,
so that their lives could be an example to the other believers in other
places. But also they preached the word in
those surrounding areas. They believed in evangelism.
They believed in reaching out with the word of the gospel
so that the word of the Lord could go out into all that surrounding area.
And this was a very common practice among the early Christians. You didn't
have to tell the early Christians to evangelize. They spontaneously
took the gospel out. The word of the Lord has sounded forth,
verse 8, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward
God has gone forth, so that we have no need to say anything.
It is our responsibility, if we have come to the Lord,
to live a godly life and then to spread forth
the word of God that has changed our lives,
everywhere where we have opportunity to. By the spoken word,
by the printed word, by every possible means,
we have to let the word of the Lord sound forth all around us.
A Christian who does not seek to spread forth and sound forth the word of
the Lord is coming short of God's purpose for his
life. And we could even say he is living in disobedience
because it's God's will that every Christian be a witness,
a spoken witness for the truth of the gospel.
And we read here, it's not only the word of the Lord that went forth,
it says here that their faith in God had gone forth in the latter part of verse 8.
Other people had come to see that these
Thessalonian Christians were people who had a living faith.
Their faith was not a dead one. It was a living faith.
And people had heard about it so that they had no need to say anything.
And Paul himself has heard reports about the Thessalonian Christians from others
in that area. And he was greatly encouraged. He says in verse 9,
For these people who speak about you, they themselves report
about us what kind of a reception we had with you.
So we see that the people who told Paul about
the Thessalonians, they themselves could tell Paul, we heard from the
Thessalonians about how you visited them.
The Thessalonians had told the others how Paul had come
and preached the gospel to them. And these others had come back and told Paul,
we've seen how the Thessalonians Christians, the latter part of verse 9,
have turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God and to
wait for his Son from heaven. Notice these three things here.
First, a true repentance. And perhaps there is no better description of repentance
in the entire New Testament than in the latter part of verse 9.
It's a turning to God from idols. And idols are not just idols of wood and
stone before which people bow down. An idol is
anything or anyone that takes the place that God should have in our life.
The place that God should have in a person's life
when it's taken by some material thing or by some other human being,
we can say that is an idol. And true repentance
is to turn from everything that takes the place that God should have in our
life. Turning from sin, turning from inordinate love to human
beings, inordinate love to material things.
This is true repentance and it's a turning
to God. And secondly, we see here after repentance and a turning to God from
idols, the purpose is that we might serve
the living and the true God. And by service, we don't mean just giving out
thanks or preaching or going out as a full-time worker.
The primary service which we can do to God, we read in Romans 12 verse 1,
is to present our bodies as a living sacrifice, wholly unacceptable to Him,
which is your reasonable service, He says there. So first of all, the
presenting of our body and then allowing God to use it in
any way He chooses. And third, to wait for His Son from heaven.
We can say the first one, turning to God from idols speaks of their faith.
Serving the living and true God was a result of their love.
And waiting for His Son from heaven is an expression of their hope
that Jesus is coming again, whom God has raised from the dead.
Jesus, who delivers us from the rock to come.
There is a lot of God that is going to come upon the whole world for its sin.
But Jesus has delivered us from it because we have put our trust in Him
who died on Calvary's cross, whom God raised up from the dead.
These three things must characterize every born-again child of God. First of
all, a faith that makes us turn from every idol
towards God. A love that makes us serve the living and the true God.
And a hope that keeps us waiting patiently, expectantly
for Jesus Christ to come from heaven when we shall see Him
and shall become like Him. We turn today to 1st Thessalonians
chapter 2. Paul writing to the Thessalonians Christian says,
For you yourselves know, brethren, that our coming to you was not
in vain. It's blessed indeed when a worker of the gospel, a Christian worker,
can say that our coming to a certain group of people
did not fail to accomplish God's purpose, that it was not fruitless.
The reason why Paul's ministry and the ministry of Silas and Timothy
in Thessalonica accomplished fruit was because of the things that we
considered in an earlier study when we looked at chapter 1 verse 5.
Because they spoke the truth of the gospel, not just in words,
but in the power of the Holy Spirit and with a life
that backed up the message. And therefore their coming to the Thessalonians
was not in vain. And that can be repeated even
in the 20th century where any Christian worker
goes forth with the truth of the gospel
according to the doctrine of the apostles in the power of the Holy Spirit
and with a life that backs up that message.
Wherever he goes in the leading of God, his going will never,
never be in vain, never be empty, never be fruitless,
and never fail to accomplish God's purpose.
And when we speak about the accomplishment of God's purpose, we do
not necessarily measure things in terms of human statistics,
in terms of large numbers, but the fulfillment
of God's purpose for a particular place. He goes on to say verse 2,
even after we had already suffered and been mistreated at Philippi,
you know we had the boldness in our God to speak to you the gospel of God
and make much opposition. Before Paul had come to Thessalonica,
we read in Acts chapter 16 that he had been in Philippi.
And there they had abused him, beaten him up,
and put him in the stocks in the jail in Philippi along with
Silas and Timothy. And the result was that the jailer was
converted. And even though they were treated so badly,
Paul and Silas particularly, who were locked up in jail,
yet when they came out they came with great boldness to Thessalonica.
They didn't get scared. They were not afraid
of similar treatment in Thessalonica. A person who seeks to serve the Lord
must be willing to face opposition and persecution. And when he faces
opposition and persecution in one place, if that robs him of his boldness,
then he is unfit to be a servant of God. God gives courage to his servants. The
spirit of fear is never from God. He says we were bold
in our God. We had courage by the help that God gave us
to come to you in Thessalonica and to tell you the
good news of God in spite of great opposition.
There was great opposition even in Thessalonica.
As we read in Acts 17 verses 1 to 9, there we read the type of treatment that
the apostles got when they came to Thessalonica. They had just come out of
Philippi, out of the Philippian jail, all beaten up.
And we read here in Acts 17 when they came to Thessalonica and Paul preached
in the synagogue for three Sabbaths, Acts 17 verse 2.
And some were convinced, verse 4, and some of the God-fearing
non-Jews were converted and the number of the leading women.
But the Jews became jealous and they got a hold of a lot of wicked men
and they formed a mob. And they looked for Paul but they couldn't find him.
They dragged Jason and some of the other believers there
out and troubled them and said Jason has welcomed these people and they
stirred up the crowd. And we read the city authorities heard of these
things in verse 8. So we find that wherever Paul went, there
was persecution, affliction, but that did not deter him from going
forth to preach the gospel. The reason was he was convinced of the
message of the gospel. He was not ashamed of the gospel.
He knew it was the power of God unto salvation
to all who believe. Verse 3 he says,
our exhortation does not come from error or impurity or by way of deceit.
No, it was the truth. There was no error in it.
And there was no impurity in it. There was no corrupt motive. They were not
preaching false doctrines and they did not have any impure motives
and they did not have any hypocrisy. As we look at this
chapter, 1 Thessalonians chapter 2, we find a tremendous picture of the type
of person a true messenger of God must be. It's not enough that our doctrine is
free from error. There must be no impurity in our motives
with which we serve the Lord. There must be no deceit or hypocrisy or
guile in anything that we say or do wherever we are.
Further in verse 4, but just as we have been approved by God
or allowed by God or having fast God's scrutiny and test
to be entrusted with the gospel. More than in one place Paul says that
God and the Lord Jesus Christ put him into the ministry
because he had been considered faithful. God has to approve us before we can
be entrusted with the gospel by him. And the greatest thing is to gain
God's approval over our life. For then the gospel we preach will have power.
And then further on in verse 4 he says, so we speak not as pleasing men but God
who examines our hearts. In Galatians 1.10 Paul said,
if I seek to please men I cannot be the servant of Christ. The one thing that
disqualifies us from being servants of Christ
is the slightest desire to please even one human being. I know somebody sitting
in our congregation or somebody reading our prayer letter or someone in any part
of the world. The moment I serve God and my service
brings out of a slight desire to please some human being,
at that moment I cease to be a servant of Christ.
And Paul said, not as pleasing men but God who examines our hearts.
It's not just a question of giving people the impression
that we are living to please God. But living before God's face
who examines our hearts, who knows what is in our hearts, what's going on within,
who knows our motives. Very important dear friends, that in all of our life and
all of our ministry we shall be able to say this, not as pleasing men but God
who examines our hearts. Further in verse 5, here again, further qualities
that should be found in any true servant of God.
We never came with flattering speech as you know,
nor with a pretext for greed. God is witness.
A person who uses the language of flattery is actually an agent of Satan
and not a servant of God. Jesus Christ never flattered anyone.
The apostles never flattered anyone. Flattery
is of the devil. And so we should never use words
to flatter people, to praise them meaninglessly.
And usually flattery is with some ulterior motive.
There are many preachers who flatter the rich in order to gain money.
And that's what he goes on to speak about, nor with a pretext for greed.
He says we didn't hide our covetousness and our desire for getting
money out of you with a pious cloak of preaching the gospel and saying nice
words to you. And he says God is witness to that.
Blessed is every servant of God who can say that everything I say there is no
desire for money from the people to whom I preach,
being the reason why I preach in this particular way.
No flattery, no desire for not only money, but any gifts from anyone.
Further verse 6, nor did we see glory from men, either from you or from others.
That comes back to what we considered earlier.
If we receive glory from men to ourselves, not only are we unfit to be servants of
Christ according to John 5 verse 44, we cannot be
among those who are counted as believers. How can you believe
we'll receive glory one from another and do not seek the glory that comes from God
alone? Jesus said in John 5 44. And so Paul said we did not seek any glory
from you. Blessed is a servant of God who can say
that we do not seek the glory or honor of any person
only to be approved by God. Further verse 6, the last part, he says as the
apostles of Christ we could have been burdensome to you.
We could have made our way felt and assumed dignity before you and used our
authority over you, but we didn't. Paul came as a servant. He was not a
Lord. He came to serve and to help, not to
Lord and to boss over others. Here is the passage of scripture worthy
of our meditation if we are seriously inclined to be true servants of God.
We turn today to 1st Thessalonians and chapter 2 and verse 7.
We were considering in our last study some of the qualities
that should characterize any true messenger of the gospel,
any true servant of the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul gives us his own example in 1
Thessalonians chapter 2. 2nd Corinthians is another book where Paul
reveals to us the type of man he was. In 1 Thessalonians chapter 2 and
Philippians chapter 3, two other passages from the Ephesus where we get a glimpse
into the life, the inner life of the apostle Paul
that made him the type of servant of God that he became, the effective,
useful Christian worker that he was. We considered in our last study
from verses 2 to 6 some of the characteristics
of Paul as a servant of God. Continuing in verse 7,
he says we were gentle among you. We behaved gently in a mild manner
in your midst. Gentleness is a very important qualification
in a true servant of Christ. Later on towards the end of his life when Paul
writes to Timothy, he says in 2nd Timothy chapter 2.
2nd Timothy 2 verse 24 and 25, and the Lord's servant must never be
quarrelsome but be kind to all people, able to teach, patient when wronged
with gentleness, correcting those who are in opposition. When people oppose us,
it becomes quickly manifest whether we have gentleness in our lives
or not. If we are quarrelsome, we are unfit to be servants of Christ.
If we don't know what it is to be kind and patient
towards those who harm us and hurt us, then we are unfit to be servants of
Christ. Paul says we were gentle among you.
And further he says as a nursing mother cherishes and tenderly cares
for her own children, thus we yearned for you and had a fond
affection for you. Verse 8, a true servant of God,
in a sense, is like a mother. And you know what all a mother has to undergo?
In order to bring forth children. It's easy to be a preacher. It's quite a
different thing to be a spiritual mother. The great lack in our country and
throughout the world is not of preachers and teachers,
it is of spiritual mothers and fathers. And a true servant of God must be a
mother and a father. Later on in verse 11, Paul says he was a
father too. But a mother as well. For example, in
Galatians and chapter 4, Paul writing to the Galatian Christians
says this. He says, I travel in birth, Galatians 4.19,
my children with whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.
That's the language of a mother giving birth to a baby.
That travail and labor that Paul went through was a travail and labor
in prayer and in concern which made him write letters to them,
which made him visit them and exhort them and challenge them,
which made him carry them in his heart in prayer and thanksgiving. Why does he
say again in labor in Galatians 4.19, he'd already
been in travail once before to bring them to the new birth
from heathenism to Christ. And now he's in labor again
for a second purpose that these born again Christians
might now be conformed to the likeness of Christ.
There's a two-fold travail that a true servant of God has
as a mother. First, to bring people to Christ in evangelism, the travail of
evangelism, and then secondly the travail of
disciple making and of leading them to conformity to the
likeness of Christ. And Paul travailed as a mother.
And you know a mother is not seeking as to what
she can get from her children, but what she can give. And this is a very
important aspect of motherhood that must be reproduced in every true
servant of Christ as a mother cares and provides for her children.
It's not the children, it's not the baby who provides for the mother,
it's the mother who provides for the baby. So he says we had a fond affection
for you. Blessed are those who have spiritual
leaders like this. Blessed are those who serve the Lord
like this, for they follow in the footsteps of Paul,
Silas and Timothy. He says we were well pleased
to impart to you, notice this, not only the gospel
but also our own lives because you had become very dear
to us. In other words, they were willing to lay down their life.
Paul, Silas and Timothy were willing to lay down their lives
to bless and help these Thessalonians Christians.
We have no right to preach to others if we are not willing to lay down our life,
sacrifice what we have, give our time, our energy,
money, everything that others might be blessed. This is so important, dear friends.
Here is the reason why many fail to be true servants of God.
They are not willing to lay down their lives. They are seeking
things from their children. They are like mothers who are seeking even from little
babies what those babies can give them. Such is
the disgraceful state of much that goes on by the name of
Christian work in many parts of the world, including our country.
But Paul was of a different type. He said
we were willing to give our lives. Then we are fit to preach the gospel when
we can say that. The reason was not for some heavenly reward.
No, it was because these Thessalonians had become dear
to Paul. He hadn't been long among them, but they had become dear
to Paul because they had turned to Christ. They were his brothers and sisters in
Christ. And the love of God flooded Paul's
own heart so that he loved them more than his own
blood brothers and sisters. Further in verse 9,
you recall brethren our labor and hardship,
our working night and day so as not to be a burden to any of you,
we proclaim to you the gospel of God. Paul's not ashamed to admit
the fact and to remind them of the fact that
he supported himself in preaching the gospel to them.
And that was possible only through his working night and day.
Paul was a tentmaker and he made tents during his spare time
sold it, thus earned his living so that he would not be financially dependent
on any of the Thessalonians Christians. He said that to the
Corinthians as we read in 1 Corinthians 9 and 2 Corinthians 11.
He said that to the elders of the church in Ephesus
as we read in Acts chapter 20. And he says it here
to the Thessalonians in 1 Thessalonians chapter 2
and verse 9. He worked night and day so that he would not be a burden to
anyone. A true servant of God must be very careful
that he's not a burden to anyone. We must never make ourselves a burden to
others financially or in any other way if we are to be true

two things that we can lose. Faith in the Lord Jesus and our love for one another. When we face
tribulation, the love of people can grow cold. They become bitter. They begin to grumble and
complain against one another. And that is in turn because their faith has gone. When faith goes,
love goes as well. These are the two things that we must safeguard in all the trials and afflictions
that we go through. Safeguard your faith in the Lord Jesus and safeguard your love for one
another and then everything is alright. And also, Timothy brought the good news
that you always have a good remembrance of us, an affectionate remembrance of us. Paul was
encouraged. He didn't seek anything from them, but he encouraged his heart that other believers
had an affectionate remembrance of him. And for this reason, brethren, verse 7, in all our
distress and affliction, we were comforted about you through your faith. In other words,
Paul says, we are going through trial and affliction here too. God hasn't allowed us to escape it.
It's not just that you people there are suffering. Paul says we're suffering too.
But the encouragement that came to us in our trial was this. What? Not that the affliction
was removed, but the news that the Thessalonians Christians were standing true in the faith.
What a man of God Paul was, that he found his encouragement in seeing the spiritual growth
of other believers. Can we say that? That we are encouraged when we see other believers growing
spiritually and that we feel sad when other believers fall or slip up? Paul had a concern.
Very often, it's the other way around with many who call themselves believers today.
They see somebody fall and they talk about it and gossip about it and they're jealous when it
goes well with someone else. This shows that such believers are carnal, probably not even
converted some of them, merely calling themselves believers. But here was a wholehearted spiritual
man who found his delight in seeing other believers firm in their faith. Notice this
tremendous statement in verse 8. Now we really live if you stand firm in the Lord.
Is that really true Paul? That your life is dependent on other people standing fast in
the Lord? There's a sense in which Paul's life was independent of everything in the world and
of everyone in the world. He was directly connected to the head, even Jesus Christ.
But because he was a member of the body, no member could suffer without Paul feeling it.
Because Paul was in close connection with the head. If we are not in close connection with the
head, then we do not suffer when other members suffer. But because Paul was in close connection
with the head, he found his life, his spiritual life surging up when others were standing firm
in the Lord. He found encouragement when he saw other believers following the Lord wholeheartedly
and facing tribulation with faith. Verse 9, for what thanks can we render to God again for you?
What return for all the joy with which we rejoice before our God on your account?
Not only was Paul encouraged, he rejoiced before God when he heard this message. He was delighted.
He forgot about all the affliction and suffering that he was going through while writing this
letter because of the tremendous joy that came to him from the good news that the believers in
Thessalonica were wholeheartedly following the Lord. Again and again we find this expression
of giving thanks to God for other believers. Here is a good practice that we can follow and
a good example to follow to give thanks for other believers. Further in verse 10,
night and day we keep praying most earnestly that we may see your face and may complete
what is lacking in your faith. There can be things lacking in the faith of others. There were things
lacking in the Thessalonians, Christians, but Paul didn't complain about that. He still gave thanks
to God for them and said, well, I'm praying that I can come sometime and fill up what is lacking.
If we see something lacking in a brother's faith, let's do something to fill it up,
brothers and sisters. Let's do something to fill it up, dear friends, not criticized and backed by it.
Then he says his burden to see these Thessalonians, Christians, he says, may our God and Father
himself and Jesus our Lord direct our way to you in God's own time. Let him remove this hindrance
caused by the devil and let him open a way for me to come to you so that I can bless you and
fill up what is lacking in your faith. And meanwhile, may the Lord cause you to increase
and abound in love for one another and for all men, just as we also do for you. Here is the great
thing in the Christian life, to increase in love. Do we have love for one another? We have to
increase in it. Do we have love for one another? Then we also need to have love for all men. We
read in verse 12, not just for all our fellow believers, but for the men around us that we
might give them the gospel and bring them also to Christ. So that, verse 13, here is the goal
ultimately, that he may establish your heart unblamable and holiness before our God and Father
at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints. If I keep myself in love for all my
fellow believers and for all men, then God will be able to establish my heart unblamable and holiness
and I shall be ready for the coming of Jesus Christ.
